title: When Codex and Claude Code Need to Talk
goal: Find builders willing to try ACC on one real dependency across independently opened coding clients and report where communication still needs human help.
audience: Engineers who already use more than one AI coding client and builders integrating agents into developer workflows.
coreTakeaway: Record coordination facts durably, distinguish delivery from attention, and verify client capabilities at the boundary where the model receives them.
bio: Mykola Maksymenko is a software engineer and the independent creator of Agents Can Communicate (ACC), an open-source local coordination layer for AI coding sessions. He builds and tests integrations between independently opened coding clients, with a focus on delivery reliability, explicit trust boundaries, and reproducible evidence from installed software. This talk shares the implementation decisions and failures behind ACC.

aiTinkerers.whatBuilt: I built ACC, an open-source local channel that lets independently opened AI coding sessions exchange questions, reviews, and handoffs across clients. Each session keeps its own conversation and permissions. In a six-minute demo, I will show a Codex session and a Claude Code session working on different parts of a registration feature, exchanging the API contract through ACC, and inspecting the delivery receipts. If the native exchange is unavailable, a reproducible replay through the real CLI will show the protocol using synthetic participants. ACC stores explicit coordination records outside the repository and requires no coordinating model. The same demo can fit a future Toronto meetup if the October programme is already full.
aiTinkerers.builderLearns: How to separate a durable message from a delivery attempt, and why an offered message or an acknowledgement cannot prove that a model completed a task. How to keep coordination useful when a client cannot wake: preserve the inbox, expose the fallback, and avoid blocking the coding session. I will explain why client support must be proved against the installed client rather than inferred from a config file. The repository includes the implementation and a CLI replay that builders can reproduce in their own agent-integration work.
aiTinkerers.technologies: Node.js 24+ and ESM, using built-in filesystem and process APIs with no third-party runtime libraries. A local filesystem store provides journalled transactions, messages, and per-recipient receipts. CLI and MCP expose coordination operations. Client hooks provide presence and next-turn context. Vendor-specific adapters handle optional, opt-in live delivery for eligible local sessions. Codex and Claude Code are the demo clients and keep their own models and provider access. node:test, mutation checks, packed-package acceptance tests, and captured real-client fixtures verify the boundaries.

summit.description:
When you open Codex and Claude Code independently to work on one feature, an interface question can still leave you copying messages between conversations. I built Agents Can Communicate (ACC) to carry those exchanges locally while each session keeps its own model, context, and permissions.

This implementation talk starts with a running cross-client workflow, then traces a question from durable recording to its recipient-owned receipt. We will inspect the architecture behind safe retries, generation-bound identity, leased claims, and capability-based delivery with an explicit inbox fallback. The session also examines failures that shaped the design: configuration that did not establish a working integration, delivery facts that could be mistaken for model attention, and hooks that repeatedly read the same backlog until they exceeded their time budget.

I will use current ACC source, installed-package reproductions, and versioned client evidence. A deterministic CLI replay makes the protocol demonstrations reproducible without model credentials. Attendees will leave with techniques for building and testing their own agent integrations, along with a small cross-client experiment they can run in their own workflow. This is a technical open-source case study, presented independently of my employer.
summit.takeaways:
1. Design a durable communication protocol that keeps send success, transport acceptance, recipient retrieval, and acknowledgement as distinct facts.
2. Make retries safe and prevent stale session generations from changing current ownership.
3. Separate certified client support, runtime reachability, and recipient consent, with a visible durable fallback.
4. Validate an agent integration through the installed package and real client, and use a mutation to show that a test detects its intended failure.
5. Measure hook costs against a growing workspace backlog and reduce repeated reads without inventing productivity claims.

reusableAbstract: Independently opened AI coding sessions keep separate contexts, even when they work on the same feature. ACC provides a local channel for their explicit questions, reviews, and handoffs. This talk follows a cross-client dependency through the running system and its implementation: durable messages, safe retries, generation-bound ownership, and per-recipient receipts. It also covers client capability evidence, visible fallback when live delivery is unavailable, and a hook performance failure caused by repeated backlog reads. Builders will learn how to verify what an agent integration actually does at the installed-client boundary and apply those techniques in their own tools.

formats.6: Four slides and one bounded live exchange, with CLI fallback. AI Tinkerers event-specific format.
formats.20: Ten selected slides, one live exchange, and core reliability lessons.
formats.35: Sixteen slides, live workflow, CLI replay, source walkthrough, and hook-cost case study. Q&A is separate.
